projects.name: Saltanimals
projects.write_up: Saltanimals is a multi-paneled work where tiny animals are hand-painted in salt water on black paper. As the water dries, the unique crystalline structure of the Dead Sea water and the Great Salt Lake water becomes visible. The properties of these salt water sources have continued to change and respond to the work's environment over the years, at times, re-liquifying, changing color, and really taking on a life of their own. Saltanimals has become the subject of a collaborative study by crystallographer Dr. Gili Cohen-Taguri and paper conservator Noa Cahaner-McManus, and our collaborative work along with two Saltanimals panels is on display at the NANO Fetter Museum of Nanoscience and Art.
projects.synopsis: Constellations of tiny animals hand-painted in crystallized salt water

projects.name: Geomagnetic Travellogue
projects.write_up:
This project follows the zero-degree line of the
earth's magnetic field from the year 1590.
It is a work in progress.

The year 1590 is significant, as it coincides with the
development of Galileo's first telescope, and with the
creation of the first compound microscope.

Therefore, my project explores incidences of macro-
and micro-scopic vision, magnetic attraction and
polarity, and the intersection of scientific, historical,
and artistic narratives.

On May 10, 2008 I made my first journey. I would attempt to go to Peru, Iceland, South Africa, and Australia.

I started my expedition in Los Angeles, and after carefully studying my maps, I plotted my destinations. I had 24 hours to make this trip.

*parallel worlds*\
*using the wrong map to get to the right places*\
*can I reach Peru through a looking glass?*
projects.synopsis: Tracing the zero-degree line of the earth's magnetic field from 1590 to the present, in five journeys.

children.name: Los Angeles
children.write_up:
I consider Los Angeles to be the starting and ending point for this journey. It is my birthplace, and I have lived here for 36 years.

California is known for its earthquakes, and Los Angeles sits upon the San Andreas Fault. This important faultline is where the Pacific tectonic plate slides past the North American tectonic plate. Half of Los Angeles is moving slowly towards Anchorage, Alaska. The other half is travelling south.

Los Angeles is home to Caltech, one of the foremost institutions in the study of seismic and geomagnetic activity, as well as astronomy and physics. Los Angeles is also home to the historical Mount Wilson Observatory, which is situated directly above my childhood home in Pasadena. This is where Edwin Hubble made many of his notable observations with the now antiquated 100-inch Hooker Telescope.
children.synopsis: Birthplace and fault line — Los Angeles as the start and end of the journey.

children.name: Cyprus
children.write_up:
- The Mediterranean island of Cyprus has been inhabited since Neolithic times. The Greeks and the Turks have been fighting over the island for thousands of years. Ironically, it is the legendary birthplace of the Greek goddess of love, Aphrodite. The name "Cyprus" is probably a derivative of the Greek word for copper, which has been mined on the island since ancient times. This is probably the reason why Aphrodite/Venus is associated with the element copper.

- It was not until November 1, 1974 (the exact day and year I was born) that a delicate peace agreement was reached for Cyprus. On this date, the U.N. drew a "green line" down the middle of the island, dividing it between the Greeks and the Turks.

- I felt a certain "geomagnetic attraction" to Cyprus — from the birthday connection with this date in Cypriot history, to the mythological, anthropological, and even geological history of the place. I found the association with a "love goddess" intriguing, as well as the importance of materials like copper and honey.
children.synopsis: A birthday shared with a divided island's peace agreement, and the myths that followed.

projects.name: The Intimacy of Physics
projects.write_up:
This series of work began with a handful of texts and images from the history of science: Galileo's experiments in physics, Captain James Cook's observations of the Transit of Venus, and various documents from the U.S. Geological Survey. I have layered these stories with my own, re-presenting and even re-enacting them in order to understand them on a more personal and direct level. This work could be seen as a desperate attempt to find hope, not in the rational certainty of science, but in its intuitive and transformative capacities.

I begin with a simple shift in the language of science, to reveal it for what it truly is: a poetry of intimacy, of falling bodies and celestial visions passing before the eyes of history.
projects.synopsis: Photographs, paintings, and objects that layer episodes from the history of science with personal narrative.

children.title: Transit of Venus
children.write_up: Between you and me something becomes visible; you are the backdrop that brings Venus into view. The "Transit of Venus" refers to the path that the planet Venus makes across the face of the Sun. When this event was observed by scientists in 1761, it became one of the earliest examples of international collaboration in the field of science. My photographs re-enact this astronomical phenomenon, but as an intimate gesture between two human beings.

children.title: Measuring the Distance at Which We Can No Longer Hear Each Other
children.write_up: When Tony and I collaborated on this art piece back in 2007, we thought we were measuring the acoustics of the desert. I asked him to hold one end of a piece of twine, and then walk into the landscape until we could no longer hear each other. Today I realize there are many distances at which people can no longer hear each other. There are voluntary distances, theoretical distances... the distances of ignorance and forgetfulness. There are geo-political distances that separate families and loved ones on each side of national boundaries; and for Tony and I, there remains the unfathomable distance of death, at which we will no longer be able to hear each other.

projects.name: Blackboard
projects.write_up:
Blackboard presents a series of photos taken in an abandoned school building in Berkeley, California. In one of the classrooms, I discovered that the blackboard had a tiny crack down the middle of it. If you stood close enough, you could see a tiny line of light shining through from the other side.

If you put your eye right up to the crack, you could see right through the crack, all the way across the next room, to an open window with sun streaming through its white curtains.

My camera was set up on a tripod, right in front of this crack. With each photo, I adjust the focus slightly, which pushes the image from a crisp view of the flat blackboard, gradually passing through the crack, across the next room behind the board, and finally ending at the open window in the distance.
projects.synopsis: A still camera in an abandoned classroom: A cracked blackboard becomes a tiny aperture, a passage between spaces and scales.

projects.name: Department of Nocturnal Affairs (DNA)
projects.write_up:
The D.N.A. is a creative project by artists Caroline Maxwell and Tal Yizrael. Envisioned as both a work of installation and performance art, the DNA functions as a speculative bureaucracy and a precarious archive. The DNA has opened field offices in various public spaces around Los Angeles and the world to collect reports of nocturnal wildlife encounters.

In addition to the ongoing collection of reports, the DNA creates artworks that respond to the issues of light pollution and the important presence of darkness in our worlds and lives.
projects.synopsis: A collaborative installation and performance project, collecting reports of nocturnal wildlife encounters, and investigating darkness as a fertile ground for knowledge and memory.

projects.name: Villa of the Mysteries: Department of Eagles
projects.write_up:
Mount Vesuvius, Roman fertility cults, and the Belgian conceptual artist Marcel Broodthaers are among the cast members of this series of work. These delicate studies are an attempt to merge the bold sensuality of ancient Roman art with the more cerebral language of late 20th Century Conceptual Art. Proposed as a series of lessons, these works present a fertility ritual for the dry, impotent climes of contemporary art.

Gouache, ink, and charcoal on paper, 9" x 12", 2007.

Jan Baum Gallery, September 2007.

projects.name: San Andreas Project
projects.write_up:
An installation at Claremont Graduate University, Oct. 30 - Nov. 5, 2006.

The San Andreas Fault is California's major earthquake fault. It is where the Pacific Tectonic Plate slides past the North American Plate. This installation interprets and misinterprets the significance of geo-tectonic activity.

children.title: Fort Tejon Corral
children.write_up: In 1857, the Fort Tejon Earthquake on the San Andreas Fault resulted in a 30-foot displacement along the fault zone. A corral built directly on the fault line was changed from a circular shape to an s-shape — broken open.

children.title: Shovello
children.write_up: A shovel, like the one used in the accompanying video, is outfitted with cello strings. The strings measure 36.9 cm., which is the average distance the San Andreas Fault has moved since the day I was born. This personal measurement now creates a specific and personal tonal range for this instrument. The San Andreas fault is a lateral strike-slip fault. The correct way to play this instrument is with lateral strike-slip movements.

children.title: Powerlines
children.write_up: Copper wires transmit power and communication over great distances in an instant. Hair grows imperceptibly slowly. An earthquake fault moves imperceptibly slowly, and on occasion, extremely powerfully. These powerlines represent both of these energies together.

children.name: Working Method
children.synopsis: How the studies for Frost Line led to the finished painting.
children.write_up:
I usually draw a room four or five times before I let myself paint it. The drawings are not preparatory in the usual sense — I'm not solving composition problems, I already know where the table goes. I'm trying to memorize the room well enough that I can paint it later without needing to look at it, the way you might learn a piece of music well enough to play it with your eyes closed.

By the time I started Frost Line, I had drawn that corner of the studio often enough that I painted most of it from memory, checking the actual room only twice, both times to confirm something about the color of the frost on the glass rather than its shape.

children.name: On Slowness
children.synopsis: A short entry on why the January Jones paintings took a full year to finish.
children.write_up:
The paintings in this room took longer than any I have made. Not because the surfaces are complicated — most of them are just a table, a window, a fall of light — but because I kept waiting for the room to tell me it was finished, and it never quite did.

I have started to think of slowness as a material, the way I think about oil or graphite. It has a texture. It resists you in a specific way. You can push against it, and sometimes it gives, and sometimes it pushes back harder, and either way you learn something about the painting you would not have learned by finishing it quickly.

I don't think fast work is worse. I think I am just not very good at it, and I have decided to stop apologizing for that.

children.name: Studio Notes, Winter
children.synopsis: Notes kept during the coldest weeks of the January Jones series.
children.write_up:
The radiator in the studio makes a sound like a held breath being let go, on and off, all day. I have started timing my brushstrokes to it without meaning to.

Some days the light comes in flat and grey and every color on the palette looks like a compromise. Other days, for maybe twenty minutes around four in the afternoon, the whole room goes the color of a bruise healing, and I try to work fast enough to catch it before it changes. I rarely do. That failure is most of what this series is about.

items.name: Correspondence with a Painter I Never Met
items.synopsis: An essay written after finding a box of unsent letters at an estate sale.
items.write_up:
# headding 1
## headding 2
### headding 3
#### headding 4
#### **headding 5**

**title 1**\
I bought the letters for four dollars, in a shoebox that also held a broken thermometer and a lot of loose buttons. They were addressed to no one in particular — drafts, it seems, rather than letters that were ever sent — and they were all about painting, in the specific, granular way that people only write when they don't expect to be read.

## part 2
I don't know the writer's name. I know she worked in a cold room, that she distrusted her own blues, and that she once spent three weeks on a single square foot of a canvas she eventually painted over entirely. I think about her more than I think about painters I actually know, possibly because there is nothing left to argue with. She only gets to be right.

images.alt: Correspondence with a Painter I Never Met
